name: Ceruchus piceus
intro: I photographed this small eastern stag beetle in the field. A decaying log can hold several stages of its life cycle, which makes the wood itself an important part of any attempt to keep it. My photograph documents an adult. The rearing suggestions below draw on its known habitat.

sections.title: Recognizing adults
sections.text: The body is glossy and black to dark reddish brown. Adult body length is approximately 10–14 mm without the mandibles. In males, look for the enlarged mandibles and a prominent tooth on the inner edge. I recommend photographing the beetle from above before it disappears back into a crevice. The mandibles and the outline of the head can then be checked together.

sections.title: Choosing wood
sections.text: Published records include decaying logs of beech, birch, black cherry, oak and red pine. When selecting material for a trial, I would start with the species and condition of the wood in which the beetle was found. Keep some intact sections as well as loose decayed wood. A field account from the Université de Montréal describes pupation within a decomposing stump. If you encounter an occupied chamber, leave the surrounding walls in place and inspect only where the cell is already visible. I have a field record for this species and no measured egg-to-adult interval from my own culture.
